justice: Spatial resources are heavily allocated to motor vehicles: multiple wide general-traffic lanes dominate the right-of-way, while pedestrian space is not clearly visible/legible in this view.

A planted median/green buffer exists between directions and along the roadside, which benefits all users indirectly (separation, greenery), but it does not substitute for dedicated space for walking/cycling.

Accessibility is uncertain: no curb ramps, tactile paving, or crosswalk curb treatments are visible from this perspective, limiting confidence that barrier-free access is consistently provided for all users.
Traffic rules appear consistent (clear lane markings and overhead guide signage), but the street design primarily favors through-movement of cars, which can be perceived as less fair for non-drivers.
safety: Clear lane markings (centerline and dashed lane lines) and overhead directional signage support predictable driver behavior and reduce navigation-related conflicts.
A landscaped median separates opposing traffic flows, lowering head-on conflict risk and providing a forgiving buffer.
Street lighting poles are present along the corridor, supporting nighttime visibility and perceived security.
However, no protected bicycle facility is visible and the roadway appears high-speed/arterial in scale, increasing exposure risk for cyclists and pedestrians near the carriageway.
livability: The corridor reads as an auto-oriented arterial (very wide roadway, long sightlines), which typically reduces street-level social interaction for all users.
There are few visible active frontages at street level; large buildings are set back and the right side includes a construction/hoarding wall, reducing everyday amenity and street activity.
Greenery is present (trees and shrubs along the roadside and median), which supports a more pleasant daily environment, but it does not create a human-scale public realm on its own.
Limited visible places to stop (no benches, kiosks, or small plazas in view) reduces opportunities for lingering and community life.
sustainability: Substantial street trees and continuous shrub planting contribute to urban greening, potential heat mitigation, and some air-quality/noise buffering.
The design strongly supports car throughput (multiple wide lanes), which can induce higher vehicle use and emissions, reducing overall transport sustainability.
No dedicated bus lane, bus stop infrastructure, or transit shelter is visible, limiting support for low-carbon mass transit in this segment.
Lack of visible cycling infrastructure (protected lane/markings) reduces the attractiveness of zero-emission cycling as a viable mode.
aesthetics: A consistent boulevard composition (straight alignment, planted median, repeated lighting poles) creates a coherent, orderly visual character.
High-rise buildings form a clear skyline and a modern city image, adding visual interest and legibility.
Landscaped edges (trees and trimmed shrubs) appear maintained and clean, improving overall visual quality.
The construction/green hoarding wall on the right introduces visual interruption and reduces streetscape refinement in that area.
comfort: Thermal comfort is moderately supported by abundant trees along both sides and landscaped planting, offering some shade and cooling (though the main carriageway remains largely unshaded).
Physical comfort for drivers appears high due to a smooth, wide roadway and clear markings; for pedestrians/cyclists it is uncertain because sidewalks/bike lanes are not clearly visible or protected.
Psychological comfort is mixed: the wide, high-speed feel and large turning/merging space can be stressful for non-motorized users even with greenery present.
Noise/air comfort may be reduced by steady motor traffic volumes implied by the multi-lane design, despite the vegetated buffers.
walkability: A walkable realm is not clearly evident: sidewalks, crossings, and pedestrian signals are not visible/legible from this view, lowering perceived pedestrian priority.
The arterial scale (wide lanes, long blocks implied by uninterrupted roadway) can increase crossing difficulty and reduce route permeability for pedestrians.
Green buffers and street trees can make adjacent walking routes more pleasant where sidewalks exist, but the lack of visible pedestrian infrastructure reduces confidence in continuity.
No visible pedestrian crossing facilities (zebra markings/refuge islands at a crosswalk) are present in the immediate foreground, limiting safe crossing opportunities.
bikeability: No protected bike lane or painted bike markings are visible; cyclists would likely need to mix with fast-moving traffic on wide lanes, reducing safety and comfort.
The roadway appears designed for higher speeds (arterial width and long sightlines), which increases perceived risk and discourages less-confident riders.
There is a landscaped strip on the right, but it functions as greenery rather than a dedicated cycling corridor; no clear physical separation for bikes is provided.
No bicycle parking or cycling-support features (bike signals, bike boxes, wayfinding for bikes) are visible, reducing end-to-end cycling convenience.
